crosslistings: First Year Course only; first day attendance required; This course begins by exploring the political history of whiteness. Our point of departure will be David R. Roediger’s newest text (2005) Working Toward Whiteness

How Maerica’s Immigrants Became White: The Strange Journey from Ellis Island to the Suburbs. We will examine how “race” has been at the core of civic assimilation. We will interrogate Roediger’s question
“…[W]hat happens when we think of assimilation as Whitening as well as Americanizing” (pp.9-10). In other words
to become American one must “fight to be White.” The core of this course will focus on post-1960 America
Yellow Power Movements. We will use autobiography
prison writings to examine the Black Power Movement
Asian American insurgency. We will end the course with an analysis of conservative people of color
their counterparts in the dominant culture
their movement to resist identity politics in the 1990s
the turn of the 21st Century. This course will be conducted in a seminar format. Consequently
critical engagement with the assigned readings
class participation are essential. This is an intermediate course
you will be expected to write three theoretical papers
using materials from outside of the course

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Psychological Anthropology
crosslistings: First Year Course only;This course explores the relationship between self
discuss critically the broad array of methods
theories anthropologists use to analyze personality
cognition in different societies. Our aim is to address questions related to the cultural patterning of personality
to understand how culture might shape ideas of what a person is. We will also seek to understand how cultures define behavior as abnormal
how to make sense of trauma
we will address the broader theoretical question related to the tension between human universals
cultural particularism. We will begin by examining the “culture
which draws extensively on Freudian models of personality
looking at issues such as culturally constituted defense mechanisms
psychological functions of religion. We will also examine psychoanalytical anthropology
learning how Freudian concepts about unconscious processes have been applied to the understanding of cultural symbols. Furthermore
in examining theories of ritual we will discuss the possible implications of psychodynamic theory

in so doing learn about some limitations of psychoanalytical theory when applied to non-Western cultures. Cognitive anthropology will be another important paradigm to be examined in the course. In this case
influenced by psychologist Jean Piaget’s theories of cognition
emotion through a conceptualization of cultural models or complex knowledge structures. The course will conclude with questions about the issue of mental health
so called “culture-bound syndromes” of the mind
body. This course will combine lectures
class discussions. It will have a strong writing component with a series of short papers
one longer final research paper. There will be one final exam. Grades will be based on written assignments in addition to oral presentations

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: 3-D Design
crosslistings: First Year Course Only; first day attendance required; Every physical object made by human hands is a work of three-dimensional design
intentional or not. Natural objects can be examined
described in terms of three-dimensional design. Most three dimensional design is essentially invisible to us
because we are surrounded by it every day
in every aspect of our lives. We do not think much about the design of our surroundings unless something seems wrong or out of place: a tree fallen in the road
a chair with too high a seat
a fork with tines too narrow
an ugly figurine on your friend's coffee table
or a barren public plaza. Conversely
successful three-dimensional design may make us feel good without our recognizing why we feel that way: a comfortable chair with a reading lamp
a 1965 Mustang. This course involves problem-solving
ideas in three dimensions. As in spoken
a vocabulary specific to the discipline can be identified
its basic elements described: in this case
elements of a visual language. By learning to recognize the basic elements of the language of three-dimensional design
we sharpen our ability to truly see our surroundings
can begin to articulate our own ideas three-dimensionally.

courses.subject: CHEM
courses.title: CSI Macalester
crosslistings: First Year Course only; From the Sherlock Holmes stories before radio to the serial radio broadcasts of mysteries
whodunits during the mid-twentieth century to the current popularity of television’s CSI: Crime Scene Investigation
society has demonstrated an abiding interest—regardless of the technological mode of delivery—in the entertainment value associated with application of systematic
analytical thinking in the course of criminal investigation. Many high-profile cases from real life have captured public attention as newspaper columnists
especially the physical evidence. The Lindberg kidnapping
the O. J. Simpson trial created stunning examples of public theatre driven by a widespread desire in people to know the facts
try the case in their own minds. Whether in an entertaining work of fiction or through an untidy twist of everyday life
forensic science serves as the fulcrum upon which collection
analysis of physical evidence lead ultimately to testimony in a courtroom. Of course
in contemporary terms the word physical is essentially a euphemism for chemical or molecular. Paradoxically
the public fascination with forensic science stands largely in opposition to the public distrust
fear of all things chemical. In this course we will work towards developing thorough
molecular level understanding of the foundations of modern forensic science. In appropriate measure

field trips may be used to guide our study of modern forensic science. Our primary text for the course will be Investigating Chemistry: A Forensic Science Perspective by Matthew E. Johll. A Short History of Nearly Everything by Bill Bryson will serve as an ancillary
very entertaining book that addresses historical aspects of planetary forensics. This course requires that you practice your written communication skills
Shoots & Leaves: The Zero Tolerance Approach to Punctuation by Lynne Truss will inform your writing mechanics.

crosslistings: Permission of instructor required; prerequisite CHEM 312. This course is an introduction to current research in the field of molecular spectroscopy. The class will engage in collaborative research with the instructor focused on recording

analyzing spectra of gaseous metal-containing diatomic molecules. One specific project this term will be to measure new electronic bands of the molecule tantalum oxide (TaO) by laser spectroscopy. If this project is successful
we plan to write up our class results for publication in the peer-reviewed scientific literature.

crosslistings: information technology are pervasive in our lives today – we live in an ever-increasing information society. For the purpose of this course we will define information technology to be general-purpose computers
applications that enable people to make good use of computing
the software that operates the computer
provides us with a human-usable interface

its applications. Because this technology permeates every aspect of our lives today

each person should be able to command a certain level of fluency with information technology that will enable him or her to use it effectively. You will obtain such fluency in this course. People with such fluency do not work in a vacuum – computers are designed to help people enjoy their lives more fully
make strides in developing new scientific discoveries
generally get their jobs done faster. Computer professionals work with data in various fields
design new applications that enable people in a wide variety of fields to make strides in many important areas. One such field is the application of computing to biological research

in particular the study of genomes. In this course we will use this particular application area to learn how to harness your new-found fluency with information technology to aid biologists with the study of genomes. To provide useful applications

courses.subject: ECON
courses.title: Principles of Economics
crosslistings: First Year Course only; The discipline of economics provides a set of analytic tools to help us understand how the world works. Provocative
economics yields insights into many different policy questions. Economics will help you to evaluate the costs
to understand how the Federal Reserve can calm financial markets. Economic analysis of the gender wage gap can help you understand why the gap exists
what we can do about shrinking it. In this presidential election year

economics can help you sort out the economic arguments of the candidates. What are the consequences of rising federal debt? Economics will help you to predict the differing effects of the candidate’s policies. The purpose of this course is to introduce you to the principal concepts of economics. After an introductory period
we will spend about half of the course discussing the basic questions of microeconomics. How do individuals in an economy decide what
how much to purchase? How do firms decide how much to produce
how much labor to hire? In the second half of the course
we will talk bout macroeconomics or how the entire economy functions. What are the economic causes of unemployment
how is it calculated? How does the federal reserve system work? This course is primarily lecture-based. Students
will find that there is ample time devoted to discussion of the subject matter
in-class problem solving. The grade will be based on homework

crosslistings: First Year Course only; In 1798 Thomas Malthus first argued that population growth would exceed food production

the redistribution of populations through international migration change the ways in which we consider this question. In this introductory population geography course we will explore global population trends
the various factors that influence the volume
distribution of populations across the globe focusing on both contemporary
historical population debates. Our objectives will be to understand the current spatial patterns of global human population distribution
how the primary components of population change (fertility
migration) differentially affect world regions. Contemporary population issues (AIDS
decisions) will provide the lens through which we begin to develop an understanding of the historical and
debates. We will examine these issues from both a macro
we will consider migration flows such as those between Mexico-US
seeking to better understand why individuals decide to move from one place to another
how changes in the global economy influence these decisions. At a local scale
we will evaluate the emergence of immigrant neighborhoods in St. Paul
Minneapolis through discussions with local experts to better understand how these new communities change the urban landscape

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Discrete Mathematics
crosslistings: First Year Course only; In this course we will explore the world of discrete mathematics. The term “discrete” is as opposed to the continuous mathematics of calculus
where objects blend smoothly into one another. In discrete mathematics
the objects of interest are finite mathematical structures that can be ordered
counted. Examples of these are Pascal’s triangle
hypercubes (the graph at the right is also a representation of a 4-dimensional cube)
derangements. One of the main topics in discrete mathematics is combinatorics
or the art of counting. In fact you might call this a course in counting. We will learn many techniques for counting the objects listed above
one of the most important ones will be recursion
induction. Our work will not be done purely for its mathematical beauty
but also for the surprising effectiveness of discrete mathematics in solving real problems. We will see applications such as airline scheduling
many of these discrete objects play a central role in computer science
the applications in that field are abundant. Your grade in the course will be based on written problem sets
exams. Some of these projects will be done in small groups
some will be done individually. We will focus on mathematical writing of several varieties: expository writing where you describe an interesting mathematical discovery
where you describe an algorithm for solving a problem
where you formally argue that a statement is true. We will also use the computer
the programming language Mathematica (which is free to you on campus) to help us illustrate ideas
solve problems. No prior programming experience is necessary.There are no formal prerequisites
but some mathematical sophistication is necessary
the kind that can be obtained through a solid high school mathematics and/or computer science program. Most important is an interest in exploring
writing about mathematics. This course is required for both the math
it fulfills the natural science distribution requirement. You can look for more information on the course website: www.macalester.edu/~halverson/math136.html

courses.subject: MUSI
courses.title: Music, Race, and Ethnicity
crosslistings: First Year Course only; Music has always been at the center of racial
the world. This course is an inquiry into the intersection of musical individuals
ethnic issues are ingrained in the production
consumption of musical sound. It explores the role of music in the deconstruction
ethnic identifications across a wide range of human societies. Students are expected to complete reading assignments from racial
ethnomusicology. Audiovisual examples are drawn from both Western
ranging from European operas to popular music in the Middle East. Students will be equipped with basic skills in analyzing
writing about music. There are no pre-requisites. This course is open to all first-year students; no previous knowledge of musical instrument or notation is assumed or required.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Ethics
crosslistings: First Year Course only; Human rights are a significant feature of the political landscape. We appeal to human rights to critique governments
in some cases to argue that armed intervention is justified. But human rights are philosophically puzzling. Do human rights such as those stated in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
the European Convention on Human Rights reflect genuine moral rights? How do we determine what moral rights we have in the first place? If there are moral rights
is there any reason to believe that some moral rights apply to all humans? Should some human rights be regarded as the rights of sentient beings
extended to non-human animals such as the great apes? In order to address these questions we will consider a variety of ethical theories including those of Kant

various contemporary philosophers. In this respect the seminar provides an introduction to ethics as well as a chance to explore the moral foundations of human rights. The emphasis of the seminar will be on critical thinking
writing. Students will write three papers on ethics
a portion of the seminar will be devoted to learning how to write a philosophy paper.

courses.subject: PHYS
courses.title: Nanoscience
crosslistings: First Year Course only; Nanoscience is the emerging field of science concerned with the control of matter on the atomic
molecular scale. This interdisciplinary field sits at the convergence of Physics
Electrical Engineering. Our course will introduce science at the nanometer length scale
their technological applications. This quantitative course will use mathematics at the pre-calculus level
includes a two-hour weekly laboratory. There are no prerequisites.

courses.subject: PHYS
courses.title: Cosmology
crosslistings: Astronomy has entered the age of "precision cosmology": recent observational results are providing remarkable constraints on models that describe the nature of our Universe. This course provides a survey of the current state of physical cosmology. The theoretical

observational elements that establish the subject as a mature science will be discussed. Prerequisites: consent of instructor; previous or current enrollment in PHYS 331; completion of PHYS 113 or PHYS 460. 4 credits.

courses.subject: POLI
courses.title: US Politics
crosslistings: First Year Course only; This course analyzes the major ideas
implementation of public policy in the United States. Throughout the course
the emphasis is on hands-on learning
active engagement with politics. To these ends
we combine course readings with political simulations
quasi-governmental organizations in action. We focus on the basic structures
functions of American government under the Constitution
structures. We also pay close attention to the 2008 presidential
focusing on the role of campaigns
voting behavior. At the end of the semester
students should be able to interpret
understand politics as they unfold in the United States. The course is built around a variety of activities that serve to facilitate
enhance students’ understanding of American Politics in action. First
we will spend some time venturing off-campus to visit
learn about local government organizations in the Twin Cities. Additionally
each student is responsible for observing one governmental or quasi-governmental organization in action
periodically reporting back to the rest of the class. Possible observation sites include campaign organizations
executive branch agencies or departments (either federal or state)
non-profit organizations. Finally we engage in a series of role-playing exercises to simulate the relationship between the President of the United States
the White House Press Corps. All students will play one of the following roles: President of the United States
or broadcast journalist. The simulation takes us through a daily briefing held by the press secretary
a follow-up press conference.The objective of this course is to equip students with a hands-on understanding of the procedures utilized by government
the complexity of public policy decision-making

courses.subject: POLI
courses.title: Legal and Political Advocacy
crosslistings: First Year Course only; It’s one thing to have a chance to speak your mind
but it’s quite another to persuade others
policy. Effective advocacy in American law
politics depends on the raw skills of communication—writing
speaking—but it begins in understanding the institutional environment in which advocacy occurs. Simply put
one must possess a sophisticated understanding of the political
legal processes in which you will take part in order for your views to have their maximum impact. This course will have you working at multiple levels: rapidly improving your oral
understanding how to author persuasive arguments
simultaneously gaining an understanding of how key decision-making institutions operate in American politics. The institutions we will explore are all around you
they make decisions that can have significant
immediate consequences on your community. We will take the opportunities presented by Macalester’s urban location in a capital city to consider advocacy before a range of bodies
from small claims courts to the Minnesota Supreme Court. What characterizes effective advocacy? What are the logics at work in the institutions
their cultures that makes some interests appear more compelling
or sensible than others? What kinds of arguments
evidence work most effectively on decision-makers in those institutions
why? This course will take on this subject by both thinking
write in the glorious abstractions of political thought
but we will also participate in the very processes that we’re studying (well

some of them anyway; hopefully we’ll stay out of court!). Ultimately we can use the perspectives of this course to turn the analysis onto ourselves: what will make you an effective participant in the life of Macalester College? What will make you an effective
engaged citizen in American civic life?

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.title: Psych of Presidential Politics
crosslistings: First Year Course only; This course will investigate the psychological concepts
dynamics applicable to U.S. Presidential politics. The focus will be on the psychological factors shaping: (1) campaigns for the office of President
how they are evaluated by voters; (2) personality qualities
leadership styles exhibited by U.S. Presidents;

policies established by U.S. Presidents during their administrations. The course will cover a number of psychological theories applicable to the political realities involving the office of President. Students will be expected to remain current with developments in the ongoing 2008 Presidential campaign. For the most part
will be used in the course. Thus
a course pack of the primary material will be made available for purchase in the first week of the class. The class will be discussion-based with many active learning exercises
movies to illustrate the concepts. New psychological theories will be introduced through lectures in which students will have an opportunity to ask questions
engage the course topics. Grades will be determined through exams focused on the primary material
periodic reflection papers focused on the ongoing Presidential election campaign will be submitted by students. Lastly
a term paper designed to synthesize all that students learn throughout the semester will be due at the end of the semester. This term paper will be in two parts
on which students will be provided feedback by the instructor.

courses.subject: RUSS
courses.title: Tolstoy’s War and Peace
crosslistings: Tolstoy volunteered to serve his country in the Caucasian wars
” as he put it in a letter. Later he studied Russia’s engagement in the early 19th-century Napoleonic wars intensely
gradually he gained fame for his polemics against imperialist wars
violence in general. But perhaps his greatest claim to fame came from his pacifist doctrine of non-resistance to evil
which has inspired people from Gandhi to Martin Luther King. Tolstoy’s stint in the South launched him as a writer of fiction. The Napoleonic wars yielded War
while he was not adamantly preaching pacifism
in which he returned to the Caucasian wars of his youth. Our course will focus on War
conclude with Hadji Murad. Over 1000 pages long
Peace has been labeled “not a novel” (Tolstoy)
it provided sustenance for numerous readers during the WWII 900-day siege Leningrad (Lidia Ginzburg). We will form our own opinion based on a thorough reading of the entire text
as well as interpretations in other media (Bondarchuk’s film
comic strips). Hadji Murad is the only Russian work Harold Bloom included in his Western Canon as “my personal touchstone for the sublime of prose fiction
to me the best story in the world.” We will look at it through the lens of the theories we studied
in the context of the current Chechen war. We will learn about the historical context of each novel
ponder such “deep questions” as the individual in relation to history
questions will familiarize us with different ways of analyzing literary texts. Writing will be a major part of the course
writing assistant can’t promise to turn each student into a Tolstoy
his writing of Hadji Murad especially will inspire our own writing: Tolstoy spent over a decade writing it
he whittled it down from twice the size of War
editing took significantly more effort than plot construction.

crosslistings: First Year Course only; first day attendance required; An introduction to the fundamental techniques of realistic acting. Through improvisation

performance. There is an indepth exploration of the craft of acting coupled with opportunities to visit institutions
while researching many styles of performance to augment your own personal growth. There will be challenges to prior presumptive theater experiences
sharing intense intimate revelations among your peers. This is a course about process; the process of learning how to write at a college level
the process of learning how to time manage homework
the process of approaching a monologue
the process of stepping fearlessly into unknown territory within the safety of our Studio Theater. All students are required to volunteer 4 hours of tech time for each stage production in the fall
as well as ushering one night. We encourage students who have little or no theater experience to take this course as a part of their introduction to the Macalester College experience.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Evolutionary Anthropology: Facts, Fantasies and Frauds
crosslistings: First Year Course only; Evolutionary anthropology is not a topic that generally comes to mind when one thinks about the greatest mysteries or debates in science. However

it could be argued that many themes of evolutionary anthropology are far more widespread than the more common scientific questions like “How did the universe form?” or “Can the laws of physics be unified?” For example

the concept of a hairy upright walking humanlike ape can be found in human cultures spanning the globe from the Pacific Northwest in North America to the Tibetan Plateau. Nothing grabs international media headlines like a Bigfoot sighting. The history of debated discoveries in evolutionary anthropology goes back many years
this class will examine some of the most widespread
as well as some of the more obscure.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: 3-D Design
crosslistings: First Year Course only; First day attendance required; Every physical object made by human hands is a work of three-dimensional design
intentional or not. Natural objects can be examined
described in terms of three-dimensional design. Most three dimensional design is essentially invisible to us
because we are surrounded by it every day
in every aspect of our lives. We do not think much about the design of our surroundings unless something seems wrong or out of place: a tree fallen in the road
a chair with too high a seat
a fork with tines too narrow
an ugly figurine on your friend's coffee table
or a barren public plaza. Conversely
successful three-dimensional design may make us feel good without our recognizing why we feel that way: a comfortable chair with a reading lamp
a 1965 Mustang. This course involves problem-solving
ideas in three dimensions. As in spoken
a vocabulary specific to the discipline can be identified
its basic elements described: in this case
elements of a visual language. By learning to recognize the basic elements of the language of three-dimensional design
we sharpen our ability to truly see our surroundings
can begin to articulate our own ideas three-dimensionally.

is widely recognized in the statistical community

many professional sports teams now employ academic statisticians to help them gain an advantage over the competition. The acceptance of sabermetrics (aided by the popularity of books like Moneyball) has led to quantitative research in other sports

as objective decision making continues to replace the haphazard “gut feelings” used in the past. The plethora of examples that are sports related are not restricted to “traditional” sports data. For example
one might wonder about the NCAA’s compliance with Title IX (a federal law which requires that men
women be provided equal opportunities to participate in athletic programs) since its enactment in 1972. This is just one of many possible topics which would constitute an excellent term project.

this course serves as an introduction both to the concept of human rights as it has developed in Western societies since the late 18th century
to the history of music in the cultures that have fostered such ideals. It intends to introduce students to the study of music (and
the arts in general) from social
using the framework of human rights as a common theme. It also aims to contextualize the discourse of human rights within the history of arts
providing students with a sense of the term’s changing meanings
across space. We will explore traditions in both Western art music (from the late eighteenth through the twentieth centuries)
twentieth-century popular music (from the mid-1940s to the present) in a search for the ways in which music has served socio-political ideologies – overtly through the aims of its composers
unintentionally through the conditions of its reception. Individual units will focus on such topics as opera in the late 18th
music in the American Civil Rights movement
representations of freedom in 20th-century piano music (Frederic Rzewski
responses to terrorism in popular music (Bjork
Wilco). A final unit will involve individual oral presentations
with students devising their own topics on the intersection of music
human rights in contemporary musical contexts of their choosing.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Problems of Philosophy
crosslistings: First Year Course only; The ancient Greek philosopher Socrates is said to have declared “the unexamined life is not worth living.” This course examines the fundamental puzzles of human life using historic texts
modern films. Some of the problems that will concern us are: What is the relation between experience
reality? What is the difference between opinion
knowledge? What is the relation between reason
faith? What is the relation between the mind

the body? Are humans free? What is the self? What is time? Is time travel possible? What is the ultimate meaning of life? What is morality? Why should I be moral? What is the best or happiest life? Along with reading classic philosophical texts by philosophers such as Plato
we will also view a number of films that address philosophical problems
Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind

so on. Although film is a very recent human invention (compared with philosophy) it seems to be an excellent medium for philosophical reflection. So we will investigate certain philosophical puzzles about the nature of film itself: Why do films engage us so deeply? Why do we enjoy terrifying films? What is the nature of time

courses.subject: PHYS
courses.title: Cosmology
crosslistings: First Year Course only; This first-year course is designed to provide a sweeping overview of the origins
fate of our universe. Beginning with the Big Bang
the cosmos underwent a remarkable series of transformations that produced “normal”
“dark” matter. Some of this matter subsequently formed into galaxies
matter is only a small part of the story: “dark energy” has been lurking in the background. We have recently learned that our universe is not only expanding
but is actually accelerating as a result of this mysterious component. To understand these remarkable changes
this course will begin with an overview of the properties of nearby astronomical bodies (e.g.
the methods that we use to learn about them. We will then discuss the Big Bang model in detail

using it to discern the characteristics of the universe when it was very young. We will conclude by extending these models forward in time with an emphasis on the ultimate fate of the universe. This course is ideal for students who are intrigued by astronomy or by the nature of the universe. The material is most accurately described mathematically; previous or concurrent experience with calculus is preferred but not required. Credit will be assigned that is equivalent to PHYS 113.

crosslistings: First Year Course only; Wealth has held an allure for many modern thinkers. The creation of a wealthy society is often associated with “civilization”
this issue has been central to the thinking of political economists since the 18th century at least. How does work create wealth for the individual
social wealth translate into individual and/or social well-being? And
how does the character of work affect individual well-being or happiness? We will examine the answers given to these questions by major writers within the political economy tradition.

courses.subject: RUSS
courses.title: Things Don’t Like Me: The Material World and Wh
crosslistings: First Year Course only; The hapless hero of Yuri Olesha’s novel Envy laments: “Things don’t like me. Furniture purposely sticks out its legs for me. A polished corner once literally bit me. My blanket
I have always had a complicated relationship...” Olesha was writing in the turbulent decades after the Russian revolution
who had just come to power
sought to abolish religion in favor of a materialist approach to life
while Constructivist artists proclaimed a new way of thinking about things
not as possessions but as “comrades.” By transforming our relationship to material objects
by envisioning them as equals rather than things to be exploited
we would ultimately transform our social relations
treat one another more humanely. A bright
benevolent future was on the horizon. Olesha’s novel is very much a product of its time
yet its hero’s plight is a universal one. We all have a contentious relationship with our material reality. The blankets are tangled
the colors of the walls are wrong
the universe is too big. Once our basic needs are met
why do we continue to adapt
how do human beings invest objects with meaning—and at what cost to others? How do the objects that surround us shape the world of ideas
other essential aspects of human existence? Drawing upon the insights of scholars from such fields as history
we will seek answers to these questions. We will read literary texts
analyze how the authors reflect as well as imagine material reality
how they deploy concrete objects to create meaning in their work.

crosslistings: ASIA 194-01; First Year Course Only; Much like the vampire
goddess are also sources of fascination in Chinese culture. This course uses the trope of goddess
ghosts to unravel the gender politics in Chinese culture. We examine how ancient
ghost to reflect changing attitudes towards gender
the female Other. Some specific topics include: how the literary representation of goddesses

its social structure; how the term goddess had been appropriated by male modern reformists for their utopian desire for modernity; how the contemporary obsession with ghost fiction/film is related to Taoist concepts
how women writers intervene within the constraints of the political
are therefore imaged as the paranoid in a paternal framework.We will take an interdisciplinary
multimedia approach to gender relations in modern fiction
other cultural genres. Students will learn the continuation
variation of Chinese tradition in contemporary contexts as well as its intersection with modern ideologies
develop critical views from gendered perspective. The course is organized thematically

courses.subject: WGSS
courses.title: Language and Gender in Japanese Society
crosslistings: LING 194-01; First Year Course only; Japanese is considered to be a gendered language in the sense that women
men speak differently from each other. Male characters in Japanese animation often use boku or ore to refer to themselves
while female characters often use watashi or atashi. When translated into Japanese
Hermione Granger (a female character in Harry Potter series) ends sentences with soft-sounding forms

his best friend Ron use more assertive forms. Do these fictional representations reflect reality? How do these distinct forms come about? Do speakers of Japanese manipulate their language to express themselves? These are some of the questions discussed in this course. Students will have opportunities to learn historical background of gendered language
discover different methodologies in data collection
find out about current discourse on language
compare gender expressions in Japanese with those in English. No Japanese language ability is required.

crosslistings: First Year Course only; In recent years

there has been a lot of public concern over the threat of emerging infections. But at what point does an infection become an “emerging" infection? It could be argued that the only thing emerging these days is public awareness of long-standing health
social problems that were previously ignored. With this perspective in mind
we will critically examine the unnatural history of infectious diseases from ancient times to the present day. We will consider the co-evolution of culture
disease: the ways that human subsistence
demographic changes have created selective conditions for new infections
antibiotic resistance. We will also devote considerable attention to global health systems viz. policies
controlling infectious diseases around the world.

courses.subject: ENGL
courses.title: Studies in Literature: Faith and Doubt
crosslistings: First Year Course only; first day attendance required; Your education at Macalester will require you to think about what you can believe
what you must doubt in ways you never have before. Here you will be exposed to beliefs that differ from your own; just as significantly
your coursework will require you to master (or at least to inhabit) the forms of skepticism
certainty that constitute academic discourses. This course
doubt as its explicit theme. Its goal is to develop your ability to reckon responsibly
powerfully with the forms of belief
skepticism that you will encounter in your college education
elsewhere. Its methods will be those of literary study
for the guiding premise of this course is that literary language is uniquely capable of resolving or requiring the deepest doubts
creating it. Our work will be to ask what specific properties of literature allow it its special powers over belief
to improve our ability to communicate about their effects. Central readings may include selections from such theoretical works as Plato’s Republic
I. A. Richards’s Principles of Literary Criticism
Wayne Booth’s The Company We Keep
Miguel Tamen’s Friends of Interpretable Objects
compromises of literary belief. We will bring our interpretive energies to bear on grand poetic creeds like Milton’s Paradise Lost
on fiction that wants us to have faith
like John Bunyan’s The Pilgrim’s Progress
fiction that wants us to have doubts
like Charlotte Lennox’s The Female Quixote
like Douglas Coupland’s Life After God. You will supplement the assigned readings with texts that emerge from your own inquiry
media beyond the scope of the syllabus into our common discussion.

courses.subject: GERM
courses.title: Vampires: From Monsters to Superheroes
crosslistings: First Year Course only; What is up with vampires these days? It seems like you run into them anytime you walk into a bookstore or turn on the TV. From the Twilight Saga to True Blood
vampires are making a comeback. But of course vampires have been popular fodder for over a hundred years

partially because vampirism can be used as a metaphor for almost anything—from the plague to sexuality to addiction. We will spend the first portion of the semester looking at “classic” tales of vampires as monsters (Bram Stoker
then look at the more recent generation of vampires (Buffy & Angel
Let the Right One In). What happened to change our imagination of vampires from monsters into hip
outsider superheroes? And what can the examination of vampires tell us about the context in which they were created? Students are required to come to class prepared
to participate actively in the classroom discussion. As preparation for class
TV shows; please note that many of the screenings will be outside of class time. In addition
students will complete weekly writing assignments
pre-writing assignments for 2 longer essays that will be required for the class.

courses.subject: GERM
courses.title: German Cinema Studies: Nazi Cinema
crosslistings: First Year Course only; The movies love to hate the Nazi
but what exactly is a “Nazi”? Whether glamorized by Third Reich propaganda
the cinematic Nazi is always a construct. This is not to say there may not be some historical
or sociological truth in the depiction of Nazis
like that of any historical group
necessarily involves construction or representation. And representations tend to tell us more about the era in which they were concocted than about the “real” thing. Consciously or unconsciously
they serve a purpose: to educate
to complicate or (over)simplify our understanding of history
or affirm us as viewers. The course will examine the questions of representation using the example of the cinematic Nazi—one case among hundreds

as the Nazi has become the symbol of evil over the past half-century. The first part of the course will focus on films from the historical period of the Third Reich. We will examine how the Nazis represent themselves in documentaries like Leni Riefenstahl’s Triumph of the Will or Fritz Hippler’s The Eternal Jew
as well as feature films like Hitler Youth Quex. We will then turn to U.S. counter-propaganda in Frank Capra’s Why We Fight
as well as in dramas like Tomorrow the World

or comedies like Chaplin’s Great Dictator or Lubitsch’s To Be Or Not To be. The second part of the course will explore postwar representations; likely examples will include William Wyler’s Judgment at Nürnburg
deals with Nazis by not dealing with them). Student obligations: a series of short papers
one longer research paper; at least one oral presentation. Two exams
a journal responding to class readings. Hopefully the Twin Cities will offer some cultural events relevant to our theme that we can visit as a class

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Intro to European History: Why Weren’t They More Like Us?
crosslistings: First Year Course only; first day attendance required; Why were people in the past so different from us? A British writer
“the past is a foreign country; they do things differently there.” Why was this true? There is plenty of evidence that they were different. For example
why did people condone so many things - absolute monarchs
etc. - that we today find deplorable? What was the matter with them? Were they morally dead?
accomplices? Our course will suggest an answer to these questions. We will do it through a case study of one concept
from the time of the French Revolution to the present day. Our working materials will be primary documents (political pamphlets
one document for analysis each week as we move from 1789 forward. Every week the “question of the week” will be: what is “justice” here
how does it compare with “justice” in last week’s document? If there is change
is it because people are having a “moral awakening” (i.e.
growing to think as we do)? Or
is it because the context of changing events
make them reshape their ideas? Is history then people’s gradual realization of what is the single
is history the result of people making choices that appear rational
even though later their choices may turn out badly
no “master plan”? There will be frequent writing assignments
but there will be a term paper (c. 15 pp.)
weekly 15-minute quizzes. I will use the Socratic method in class
but there will also be individual student reports
web exercises. The course will meet for one hour three times per week. It satisfies your first year seminar
it will count for a history major

crosslistings: First Year Course only; cross-listed with AMST 222-01; first day attendance required; Macalester College sits on the banks of the Mississippi River which
for most of United States history
has been considered the dividing line between East
West. This class investigates the ways different groups of Americans
experienced the land west of the river. Fantasies about the U.S. West are central to American history
collective memory. Ideas about the West have shaped the ways we think about settlement
we will examine the myths that have circulated about the West alongside what has been called "new western history."

crosslistings: LATI 394-01; This course investigates the historical tendency to build cultural

political bridges across national borders in Latin America while also interrogating the import of the nation-state as the primary force for building collective identities in the postcolonial era. We will read
discuss classic texts considering the possibility of a pan-Latin American identity by figures such as Simon Bolivar
or Jose Vasconcelos as well as a growing body of critical literature endeavoring to trace the transnational
Pacific ties of Latin American cultural
political movements. Contemporary figures like Eduardo Galeano
the latest strain of Bolivarianism epitomized by Venezuela's Hugo Chavez will also be discussed as part of this living tradition of thinking "beyond the nation."

courses.subject: HMCS
courses.title: Screens
crosslistings: First Year Course Only; We spend our lives staring at the screens of computers
televisions. And the amount of time we spend before them is anything but insignificant. According to a recent study by the Kaiser Family Foundation
8-18 year-olds devote an average of 7 hours
38 minutes using entertainment media across a typical day (more than 53 hours a week)! Because they spend so much of that time "media multitasking" (using more than one medium at a time)
they actually manage to pack a total of 10 hours
45 minutes worth of media content into those 7½ hours. The screen is one of the most important technological innovations of recent memory
for it has such a wide range of influences on our experience of the everyday. From online social networking to television news
our experience of the world is largely mediated by screens. They shape our understanding of it by framing the world in a display of colored lights. Given this dependence on screens
what impact do they have on our perception of the news
contribute to what Anne Friedberg has called a "dematerializing of reality"? Do we have reason to be worried about their pervasiveness? In this First Year Seminar
related questions. We will begin to develop our own answers to them by reading
making our own content for screens. This course is designed to familiarize students with college-level writing
so there will be frequent short written assignments as well as a longer research paper. In addition

content producers. From small screens (the Apple store at the Mall of America) to extra large screens (at 5200 square feet

medium sized screens (video art at the Walker Art Museum) to old screens (a camera obscura in St. Paul)

sizes. This class will introduce you to the field of Media Studies
help you come to an understanding of the importance of screens in mediating our experience of

courses.subject: MUSI
courses.title: Music and Freedom
crosslistings: First Year Course only; first day attendance required; The concept of freedom both lies at the heart of human rights discourse
provides the spark that ignites any number of musical movements. Intended for students with strong interests in the intersection between the performing arts
this course serves as an introduction both to the concept of human rights as it has developed in Western societies since the late 18th century
to the history of music in the cultures that have fostered such ideals. It intends to introduce students to the study of music (and
the arts in general) from social
using the framework of human rights as a common theme. It also aims to contextualize the discourse of human rights within the history of arts
providing students with a sense of the term’s changing meanings
across space. I take “freedom” to signify a number of ideals
it is the intention of this course to expose students to this diversity

opening more questions about music’s relationship to human rights than providing answers. We will explore traditions in both Western art music (from the late eighteenth through the twentieth centuries)
twentieth-century popular music (from the mid-1940s to the present) in a search for the ways in which music has served socio-political ideologies – overtly through the aims of its composers
unintentionally through the conditions of its reception. Individual units will focus on such topics as opera in the late 18th
music in the American Civil Rights movement
representations of freedom in 20th-century piano music (Frederic Rzewski
Radiohead). A final unit will involve individual oral presentations
with students devising their own topics on the intersection of music
human rights in contemporary musical contexts of their choosing. No prior background in music is required for the course
although it is assumed that any student taking this course will have a true interest in a variety of musical traditions
including not only familiar popular styles

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Modern Political Philosophy
crosslistings: First Year Course only; first day attendance required; John Rawls wrote
“Justice is the first virtue of social institutions
as truth is of systems of thought. A theory however elegant
economical must be rejected or revised if it is untrue; likewise laws
institutions must be reformed or abolished if they are unjust” (A Theory of Justice). While there would be general agreement with such claims about the importance of justice
there is much less agreement about what makes a society just or unjust. In fact

radically different conceptions of a just society have been developed within the tradition of Western political philosophy. In this course we’ll look at some of the most influential ideas about a just society
the first major development of the idea of justice in Western philosophy
arguably the most important political philosopher of the twentieth century. In between we’ll also read works of at least the following: Thomas Hobbes
John Stuart Mill. Course requirements will consist of four short (5 to 7 page) papers
some of which will be written in two drafts
written reactions to readings to be done before the readings are discussed in class.

a number of major scholarly texts. The primary goal of the course will be to develop a substantive understanding of the phenomenon of “world order/world order transformation”
as a foundation for the further study of international politics. Emphasis will also be placed on developing a range of critical
communication skills required for the further study of international politics. The course is thus intended to prepare students for advanced work in the field
although it should be appropriate for those merely seeking to satisfy an interest in the study of global politics.

crosslistings: Tolstoy volunteered to serve his country in the Caucasian wars

violence in general. But perhaps his greatest claim to fame came from his pacifist doctrine of non-resistance to evil
which has inspired people from Gandhi to Martin Luther King. Tolstoy's stint in the South launched him as a writer fiction. The Napoleonic wars yielded War
while he was most adamantly preaching pacifism
in which he returned to the Caucasian wars of his youth. Our course will focus on War
conclude with Hadji Murad. Over 1000 pages long
Peace has been labeled "not a novel" (Tolstoy)

as well as interpretations in other media (Bondarchuk's film
comic strips). Hadji Murad is the only Russian work Harold Bloom included in his Western Canon as "my personal touchstone for the sublime of prose fiction
to me the best story in the world." We will look at it through the lens of the theories we studied
in the context of the still simmering Chechen war. We will learn about the historical context of each novel
ponder the individual’s relation to history
questions will familiarize us with different ways of analyzing literary texts. Writing is a major part of the course
writing assistant can't promise to turn each student into a Tolstoy
his writing of Hadji Murad especially will inspire our own writing: Tolstoy spent over a decade writing it
he whittled it down from twice the size of War
editing took significantly more effort than plot construction.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Refugees/Humanitarian Response
crosslistings: First Year Course only; This writing-intensive seminar uses anthropology to situate the experiences of refugees
other forced migrants within a global framework of conflict
humanitarian response. Through analysis of select case studies
we will probe the complex interplay of social
economic factors that are invoked to explain modern refugee-producing conflicts. We will consider how refugees act
are acted upon in these settings
in their aftermath. We will examine critically the ways refugees are defined
as such discourse determines access to certain entitlements
governmental responses. We will consider how refugees are defined in terms of time
space as transnational actors. Once we have a better understanding of the nature of the collective experience of war
we will consider issues of power
human rights embedded in humanitarian responses to conflict by examining the roles of those who engage in humanitarian work in U.S.
international settings. Our scope of inquiry includes humanitarian workers broadly conceived
others. In addition to probing the ways that outsiders react to refugee concerns
we will also examine indigenous institutional coping mechanisms—such as family
religion—that facilitate social reconstruction in times of transition. The format of the course will be in-depth discussion
a field research project that will involve cultural life history interviews with an individual engaged in humanitarian work

systems of globalization that shape our world today. In this seminar
we will also place these pandemics in the context of our globalized lives
chart a path forward for global public health as human population climbs toward 10 billion on a steadily warming planet.

courses.subject: CHEM
courses.title: General Chemistry I: Structure and Equilibrium
crosslistings: First Year Course only; This course provides a rigorous treatment of the concepts foundational for all subsequent study in chemistry. This course
which is typically taken in the spring semester of the first year
together satisfy the prerequisites for Organic (CHEM 211)
Analytical (CHEM 222) Chemistry. The first two-thirds of the class is devoted to understanding the properties of individual atoms
how atoms bond together to form the three-dimensional structures of molecules. Our detailed examination of atoms
molecules will draw upon insights from the most important scientific theory of the 20th century—quantum mechanics. In particular
quantum mechanics will help us explain electronic structure
the ways electrons distribute themselves in atoms
molecules. We will also explore how the structure of individual atoms
molecules can help explain the bulk properties of macromolecules

materials. The last third of the class focuses on the concept of equilibrium. Equilibrium can be defined as the ultimate outcome of a physical process or chemical reaction. We will learn how to describe physical
chemical equilibria mathematically. We will also interpret our mathematical results in terms of the structure
bonding concepts learned in the first part of the course. We will pay particular interest to the chemistry of acids
which are immensely important for any future study of organic

courses.subject: COMP
courses.title: Computing and Society: The Data and Digital Media Revolution: the Next Big Thing in the Liberal Arts
crosslistings: First Year Course only; In one sense
we can think of digital data such as text files
images as something to be read or viewed by humans. In another sense
we can view these files as something to be studied computationally. For many
researchers in the humanities studied manuscripts
other media created by humans in an effort to study the human condition. In the past decade
some humanities scholars have begun integrating technology into their research by studying digital representations of documents that were not originally created digitally
along with more recent documents of digital origin. These documents
once meant for individual human viewing
can now be studied by humans using computational tools such as algorithms
data visualization. The surge in availability of digital documents enables us to create computational tools to analyze large amounts of data (much more so than can be done by an individual)
learn more about it than we could by simply reading it. Thus
the new field of Digital Humanities has begun. In this course we will begin to learn how to create the computational tools needed to analyze data
sound data from the humanities as examples.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Introduction to Latin America and the Caribbean
crosslistings: First Year Course only; cross-listed with LATI 181-01; Is it possible to properly describe a complex
heterogeneous region that ranges from the US Southwest to Tierra del Fuego under an invented nineteenth-century French term such as "Latin America?" Why or why not? What are the political
cultural implications of such a flattening of the hybridity of this vibrant
complex part of the world? And just how does the whole process of colonialism
neocolonialism fit into this picture? These are some of the questions we will address in this course
which presents a roughly chronological survey of Latin American history. Given its broad scope

the course emphasizes three critical moments. The first concerns the great upheaval of the conquest with an emphasis on the sixteenth-century establishment of a “colonial” order. The second traces the dissolution of this society
the transition to national states with an emphasis on the twin conceits of "science"
"progress." The third emphasizes the twentieth century with special attention to the rise
the role of the United States as patron

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Math and Society: Newton’s Principia
crosslistings: First Year Course only; The year is 1600. Advances in technology have forced a handful of philosophers— Francis Bacon
Galileo Galilei among them—to begin a systemic re-evaluation of how to study the world: what questions should be asked
what answers are acceptable. By 1800 this "scientific approach" will have been articulated
in its ability to lead the way to human progress will hav become a fixture of Western civilization. What happened? Why did it happen? And wha can this tell us about our societies today
the changes they are experiencing? While this course will consider the full sweep of the Scientific Revolution from 1600 to 1800
it will focus on one pivotal event: the publication in 1687 of Isaac Newton's The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy. This is a work of physics
philosophy that revolutionized each of these areas. We will investigate its genesis
follow some its repercussions as it takes on a mythic nature that shapes the Age of Enlightenment.

courses.subject: MUSI
courses.title: Songs
crosslistings: First Year Course only; first day attendance required; Music is ubiquitous in our lives: we are bombarded by advertising jingles
shows reflecting a multitude of genres. Music is more easily obtained than ever
other online sources. We can talk enthusiastically about the songs we like
we freely criticize those we don't. We may not realize
that the meaning of the word "song" has become corrupted to mean any kind of music
when really the term refers to something more specific: music that is sung. Songs have to have words
in this course we will trace the development of vocal music throughout history. Our central thesis will be

"How does this music communicate with the listener?" Of course the lyrics confront us with often very direct meanings. But what about the music itself? What were composers trying to convey? How can music be emotional? How can it communicate social
political ideas? How can it stir the imagination
soul? Not all vocal music is technically a "song." We'll look at choral music
plenty in between. We'll limit our study to the music of the Western world (Europe
quite a bit of the core repertoire will fall under the umbrella of "classical music
" which makes sense since what we call popular music has only been round for about 60 years now – there are 1
000 years of musical development before that to take into consideration. Occasionally we'll make forays into the arena of purely instrumental music
so as to study further musical styles
become thoroughly acquainted with musical creators

courses.title: Introduction to Philosophy: Philosophy and Film
crosslistings: First Year Course only; Film seems to be an especially vivid
effective medium for the exploration of fundamental philosophical questions. And the medium of film raises interesting philosophical questions in its own right
aesthetic experience. This class will combine reading of classic
classic films. The texts will include writings by Plato
Nietzsche. The films may include Rashomon
Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind
so on. Some of the main philosophical questions we'll examine are: What is the relation between experience
reality? What is the relation between reason
faith? What is the relation between the mind

the body? Are humans free? What is the self? What is time? Is time travel possible? What is the ultimate meaning of life? What is morality? Why should I be moral? What is the best or happiest life ? Why do films engage us so deeply? Why do we enjoy terrifying/violent films? What is the nature of time
space in film? Can we 'do philosophy' with film? Are directors philosophers?

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Introduction to Philosophy: Philosophical Persons: Persons and Personal Iden/Philosophical Tradition
crosslistings: First Year Course only; When Descartes proclaimed "I think
therefore I am" he seemed to be saying that
even in the midst of doubt
he could be certain of at least one thing

the existence of his own self. Yet not many years later Hume argued that however much he examined the nature of his own experience he never encountered any entity that might be labeled "the self." Descartes
Hume disagreed about the nature of the self
makes one the same self over time. Thus began one of the enduring debates of philosophy
the nature of selves or persons
personal identity (the problem of what makes us the same person through time). This philosophical question strikes at the nature of our existence
remains central to our intellectual life
not only for professional philosophers but for anyone curious about his or her own existence. Perhaps you hav wondered about what connects you to yourself as a young child
or to a future self twenty years from now. In this course the problem of defining persons
the nature of personal identity will be used as a basis for exploring the wider philosophical tradition
methodologically. Students will study a variety of philosophical topics that flow naturally from a consideration of the nature of persons
to include: mind-body dualism; free will
determinism; artificial intelligence; our responsibility to other non-human animals; beginning
theories of life after death. The texts for the course will consist of both classical
contemporary philosophical texts of important Western
texts from non-philosophical sources. Participants will thus become well versed in the different methodologies used to answer philosophical questions.

courses.subject: POLI
courses.title: International Politics
crosslistings: First Year Course only; This first year course is designed to introduce students to the field of International Relations. As an introduction to the field
it has three broad goals. The first is to develop the foundational knowledge
conceptual literacy necessary to engage with the field’s multidimensional concerns. These include global order

human rights. The second is to introduce students to the different perspectives or intellectual frameworks for making sense of international relations (also known as global or world politics). The third goal is to develop a range of critical
writing skills for more advanced work within the field. We will pursue these goals through an examination of contemporary International Relations scholarship
including texts on the role of the United States
international peacebuilding in the Democratic Republic of the Congo
domestic service in the political economy of Southeast Asia
as well as through different types of writing assignments

crosslistings: First Year Course only; cross-listed with LATI 141-01; first day attendance required; Latin American women have overcome patriarchal "machismo" to serve as presidents
human rights activists. Through a mix of theoretical
we will explore issues such as feminist challenges to military rule in Chile
civil war in Colombia. Teaching methods include discussion

a biographical essay. This class employs an innovative system of qualitative assessment. Students take the course "S/D/NC with Written Evaluation." This provides a powerful opportunity for students to stretch their limits in a learning community with high expectations
but without a high-pressure atmosphere. This ungraded course has been approved for inclusion on major/minor plans in Political Science

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.title: Psychology of Immigration and Acculturation
crosslistings: First Year Course only; While migration
border crossings have existed since the beginning of human history
the accelerated rate of globalization in the past decades has introduced new issues for identity
community. This course explores the psychological processes involved in moving into an unfamiliar culture
both for those who accomplish the relocation (and subsequent generations)
for those already present in the receiving country. We will read book chapters
journal articles focusing on the psychology of immigration
acculturation in a wide range of countries
discuss topics such as ethnic enclaves
identity confusion. Upon exploring the general model of acculturation
we will discuss emerging phenomena such as multiracialism
return migration. Course assignments will include short written responses to the readings

courses.subject: RUSS
courses.title: "Things Don’t Like Me": The Material World and Why It Matters
crosslistings: First Year Course only; The hapless hero of Yuri Olesha’s novel Envy laments: “Things don’t like me. Furniture purposely sticks out its legs for me. A polished corner once literally bit me. My blanket
I have always had a complicated relationship...” Olesha was writing in the turbulent decades after the Russian revolution
who had just come to power
sought to abolish religion in favor of a materialist approach to life
while Constructivist artists proclaimed a new way of thinking about things
not as possessions but as “comrades.” By transforming our relationship to material objects
by envisioning them as equals rather than things to be exploited
we would ultimately transform our social relations
treat one another more humanely. A bright
benevolent future was on the horizon.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Criminal Behavior/Social Control
crosslistings: First Year Course only; Imprisonment as a form of criminal punishment is only about as old at the United States. By 2009

over 7.2 million people in the United States were under correctional supervision – equivalent to 3.1% of the adult population. How should we understand the growth of this form of criminal punishment? In what ways is it similar to other methods of attempting to control unwanted behavior? What insights can a sociological approach offer on these questions? In the first volume of the American Journal of Sociology over 100 years ago
Edward Alsworth Ross published an essay on the topic “Social Control

” arguing for the importance of sociology as a moral science that could provide unique insight about “the moral upbuilding of [people] going on under the guidance of society” that makes possible “ordered social life” (1896: 535). Ross was hardly alone in his convictions

representing the dominant understanding of early American sociology as a science that could help build a better society by providing knowledge that could be used to reform social ills. Over the ensuing century
social control practices grew to be far more formal
witnessed by the growth of specialized institutions

crosslistings: First Year Course only; first day attendance required; The Twin Cities of Minneapolis

artistic institutions. In this class we attend to many aspects of performance in the vibrant Theatre
Performance communities -- including Dance -- of the Twin Cities. We will attend theatre
dance performances throughout the city as a group
study the genres of their crafts through the examination of texts
performance in the classroom. The course meets once a week (Wednesday night)
in order to facilitate a schedule of evening excursions
on-campus seminars. The viewing of performances alternates with campus classroom seminars (sometimes every other week
or every second or third week)
reflect on their enactments in performance
learn about the key terminologies for the poetics of work in performance
develop our capacities for interpretational strategies in the performing arts.

courses.subject: WGSS
courses.title: Gender and Sport
crosslistings: First Year Course only; first day attendance required; This course sets out to investigate ‘modern sport’ largely (though not exclusively) within the context of the United States. As a major social institution
sport functions as a microcosm of society
one that illuminates quite powerfully the larger
structures operating in our world. Sport as we know it is a relatively modern institution
a product of industrialization that took shape over the course of the 20th century. Like all social institutions
sport is driven by contemporary global capitalism
relying in turn as it does on notions of the “natural”—a notion that will be continuously contested throughout the semester. In short
sport is constitutive of contemporary life
is a core (and visceral) component of our culture (our “way of life”). Sport has been
an expression of hegemonic masculinity. Sport
sporting culture have thus greatly shaped (and rigidified) the (hetero)gender binary. While sport works to maintain our gender normative structure
we will also investigate ways in which sport (potentially) challenges dominant notions of “masculinity”/ “femininity”
binarized gender. Employing a critical lens through which to investigate sport
a central task of this course will be to investigate
using a variety of theoretical frameworks—such as feminism
critical race scholarship—the intersections of gender
sexuality as it relates to sport. Our objective as a class thus involves understanding
dissecting the ways that sport maintains

courses.subject: ENGL
courses.title: Novel
crosslistings: This course focuses on the novel as a literary form. British novelist John Fowles has said
"novelists write for countless different reasons: for money
for amusement: as skilled furniture makers enjoy making furniture
as Sicilians like emptying a shotgun into an enemy's back. I could fill a book with reasons
though not true of all. Only one same reason is shared by all of us: we wish to create worlds as real as
but other than the world that is." Thinking of Fowles' view
coupling it with many other attitudes toward that bulky grab-bag known as the novel
we will explore the genre via six books. We begin with Frances Burney's Evelina (1778)
Virginia Woolf's Mrs. Dalloway (1925) which furnish examples of an eighteenth-
a twentieth-century novel. We then backtrack slightly to Henry James's What Maisie Knew (1897)
before moving ahead again to Vladimir Nabokov's Lolita (1955)
Maria Beig's Hermine: An Animal Life (1984). These latter three works offer thematic connections of interest
all six novels feature an eponymous heroine (if “heroine” is the word). The authors include two British writers
one Russian writer transformed into an American
one American writer transformed into an Englishman. Each work will be considered as a constructed artifact
as the reflection of a particular moment in time
as a commentary on what it means to be human. Students submit a combination of papers
periodic objective quizzes manifest themselves along the way. The class is discussion-based

crosslistings: First day attendance required; ACTC student may register on December 4th with permission of the instructor; This course will cover research design
with a focus on practical issues. Research design topics will include pseudoreplication
specialized experimental designs. Data analysis topics will cover univariate statistics – from simple tests to modeling with multiple explanatory variables – non-parametric statistics
multivariate methods such as Principal Component Analysis. The major aim of the course to have students gain competence
confidence in the analysis of biological data - selecting appropriate statistical tests for particular questions
generating a useful 'dialog' with their data. Prerequisite: Math 155

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Cold War Latin America
crosslistings: Latin America was a decidedly “hot zone.” This class examines the reasons for this phenomenon
external pressures such as the region’s sociopolitical instability
its conflictive relationship with the United States. The class will examine some of the more dramatic moments of the Latin American Cold War
including the overthrow of Jacobo Arbenz in Guatemala
we will engage less-discussed elements of the Latin American Cold War such as its important role in fostering transhemispheric solidarities
the creative possibilities of Cold War cultural production
the emergence of a youth counterculture
the many attempts by Latin Americans across the political spectrum to reject the premise of the Cold War altogether.
